content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper solves the problem of unsupervised domain adaptive object detection. They proposed a method on top of Strong-Weak alignment (Saito et al., 2019). In this previous work, two losses are proposed, a weak-alignment loss for global features and strong-alignment loss for local features. In addition, the previous work proposed to utilize context-vector for effective object detection. 

Their contributions of this paper are summarized as follows.
1, adversarial alignment losses for low-level features by adding domain classifier to many low-level layers
2, adding context features from the low-level features 
3, they proposed to detach the gradient from the context features to avoid a negative transfer.  
4, the effectiveness of their method is validated through extensive experiments on many object detection datasets. 

I lean toward rejecting this paper from the following weakness.

1, Their method lacks technical novelty to accept. Adding many domain classifiers to lower-level layers and adding more context vectors are just minor modifications to Strong-Weak alignment (Saito et al., 2019). In Strong-Weak alignment (Saito et al., 2019), the idea of performing adaptation in multiple-layers and using context-vector are proposed. In Chen et al., 2018, using instance-level features for alignment is proposed. Although the use of these techniques is a slightly different from these existing works,  the difference is too minor. 
2, The presentation is poor, especially in the introduction. For example, they introduced COL in the introduction. However, I could not see a close connection with this paper. In "Our key ideas" part, it is also unclear what was the key idea and novel idea.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable and helpful comments. Below we make further clarification to each concern from you:

Q1: Their method lacks technical novelty…
A1: We insist our method has many technical novelties like gradient detach on stacked diverse losses, which are quite different from previous papers. We also want to clarify that our key ideas do not lie in “Adding many domain classifiers to lower-level layers and adding more context vectors”. We believe there may be some misunderstandings from you on our paper. In summary, two main points/contributions are developed in this paper. First, the purpose of this paper is to explore the incorporation of different objective formulations. We have provided extremely comprehensive experiments and ablation studies to verify this. Second, we use detach-based updating strategy to learn more discriminative representations. Furthermore, these two techniques are symbiotic and can help with each other in the framework (you can refer to our Table 1). They are also the reasons why our method can obtain fairly competitive results to exceed all previous SOTA methods. 

A2: They introduced COL in the introduction. However, I could not see a close connection with this paper. In "Our key ideas" part, it is also unclear what was the key idea and novel idea. 

Q2: COL is proposed to use complement loss for neutralizing the probabilities of the complement classes (the target data in our case), which, at least has two aspects that are very close to our method. 1) complement and main losses for better cooperation; 2) complement classes/data for better utilization. The differences are that we use detach-based strategy to update the gradient and diverse complement losses. Despite these, we still have similar motivation and goal in spirits, that’s why we put COL in the introduction as a reference. We have revised this part in our paper with the similarities and differences to make it more natural.

For our key idea and novelty, as we mentioned for R2, R1, in essence, there are two main components proposed in this paper: 1) stacked complementary losses and 2) gradient detach updating. 

Each component, if taken alone, 1) may be similar to strong-weak alignment and MAF to some extent if compared roughly, since they also use multi-objective for training. However, the inside design and motivation are different: Our method is motivated from deep supervision, but we make a further step to adapt multiple and diverse losses. In contrast, strong-weak adopted local and global branches and hasn’t explored whether stacked losses can further help to optimize the model. MAF applied multi-loss on Block 3, Block 4, Block 5 with the same formulation. As we mentioned in the abstract and introduction, this design cannot deliver a sufficient integration within different domains in the shallow layers. Thus, our work is truly deeper than all of these literature. 

From our results we can get the insight that domain adaptive object detection is supported by deep supervision, however, the diverse supervisions should be applied in a controlled manner.

2) is completely new and novel for this task in our view. We didn’t find any previous work that has the same or relevant definition of it for domain adaptive object detection. The closest work may be the h-DETACH [1] while it has a quite different manner and motivation with an irrelevant problem (sequential tasks). We observe this operation can help to learn more discriminative features after we have studied and visualized a very large variety of heatmaps, also we aim to maximize the information of context from the raw images to help the detector. Strong-weak chooses to use features after GRL layer, which, in our opinion, may weaken the strength of information from the input image. The proposed operation is simple, but this is a very effective and efficient way to achieve our goal. We tend to keep our method as simple as possible so that it can make a good benefit and wide usage for relevant researches.
Also, gradient detach updating is the optimal companion for stacked complementary losses and they are complementary in our whole framework, our title also reflects this fact.

Furthermore, our result is competitive which outperforms the strong-weak alignment (CVPR’19) and MAF (ICCV’19) on the popular FoggyCityscapes benchmark by absolute 3.6% and 3.9% mAP (Our result is 37.9%, previous SOTA is ~34.3%, the upper bound performance, with ground-truth boxes on target domain, is 40.3%). This demonstrates that our design is more reasonable than MAF and strong-weak methods. We think how to use the correct way in designing a complicated framework to obtain desired performance should also be a novel point and important contribution to this task, and it can even benefit the whole community as we have released the code.

We also have revised the relevant parts (introduction, method, etc.) and whole paper to make them more clear. Please check them out.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper introduces a new algorithm for learning to detect objects in two domains (eg. sunny and night images), in which one domain is labelled (object categories and bounding boxes) and the other domain does not have labels. To do so, the paper introduces a neural network trained with multiple loss functions and a modified gradient update similar to (Arpit et al., 2019). The method achieves few percentage better accuracy than state-of-the-art methods.

The problem of domain adaptation is of crucial importance and seeing improvements is exciting. Yet, I find the following points not convincing: 

-Novelty: The algorithm in the paper is strongly based on the network introduced by (Ren et al., 2015) with the domain adaptation strategy of (Chen et al., 2018; Saito et al., 2019). The novelty of adding additional loss functions and adapting the gradient update of (Arpit et al., 2019) seems prima facie incremental. 

-Analysis of the approach: It is unclear from where the effectiveness of the approach comes from. Figure 1 visualizes the features in the two domains with tSNE, and the features from this paper and from (Saito et al., 2019) have the same properties. From the figure it can not be concluded that "our feature embedding results are consistently much better than previous approaches" as the caption says. The ablation study in Table 1 seems to indicate that the gradient update almost does not bring any improvement and it is unclear what else can be learnt from this analysis. In the text of the paper nothing is mentioned. Finally, the attention maps in Figure 6 show no differences with or without detached gradients, but the description of this figure in the text is not in accordance to what is shown in Figure 6.

-Incremental accuracy improvements: Also, when looking closely to the final accuracies, they are  ~3% larger than the best published results which contradicts one of the conclusions "Our experimental results outperform the state-of-the-art approaches by a large margin on a variety of benchmarks” (ie. 3% is not a large margin). 

-Generality of the approach: The algorithmic improvements presented in this paper are specific for object detection and it is unclear if these ideas would transfer to other domains and how.  In fact, the algorithmic choices are described but not derived from some principles, ie. the paper justifies the algorithmic choices because they are "simple yet effective” and presents them as a series of steps to follow. This obscures how the approach is connected to previous works and how to use it in new works.

In summary, the paper tackles an important problem and shows few percentage improvements over state-of-the-art accuracy but the method is based on modifications of previous works that are not well justified.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer1 [2/2]
content.comment:
Q2: Analysis of the approach: It is unclear from where the effectiveness of the approach comes from; no differences on tSNE embedding and attention maps.
A2: For tSNE embedding: if you zoom in the figure of “from Cityscape to FoggyCityscapes” embedding, you will observe that there are some points in strong-weak (CVPR'19) embedding which are not aligned (i.e., red and blue can be seen). However, embedding in our case the alignment is obviously much better (all points are in purple color, indicating source and target align completely) than all others.
As we mentioned above, losses and gradient detach are complementary to each other. So if you see the combination of different losses (in presence of detach) in table 1 and table 9, it can be verified the given set of losses outperforms other combinations. And if you check any combination of losses with detach and without detach, you can observe that with detach always has better performance.

For attention maps: As mentioned in the response to reviewer 2, on comparing with two heatmaps it can be seen that “without detach model” focuses more on background (green color) as compared to “with detach model” (blue color, i.e., less attention)

For the analysis of the approach and where is the improvement from, we clarify that the effectiveness is mainly from our proposed two components: 1) stacked complementary losses and 2) gradient detach updating. We have reorganized Table 1 which clearly demonstrates this statement, so you can check there for more details. We have also included more discussions in the revision.

Q3: Incremental accuracy improvements, ie. 3% is not a large margin.
A3: Our result on FoggyCityscapes is 37.9%, previous SOTA is 34.3%/34.6%, the upper bound performance is 40.3% (meaning that it uses ground-truth on target domain for training). Our method obtains 10.5%/9.5% relative increase. We think this is a fairly significant improvement.

Q4: Generality of the approach
A4: If you mean that the generality is to generalize our method to other tasks except for object detection, we think our idea of gradient detach can be tried to apply to those visual tasks that rely heavily on the discriminative context information, like semantic segmentation, image inpainting, etc. to learn a better representation. If you mean generality within the same task, our method is highly modular, so from our viewpoint, it’s still easy to plug into other domain adaptive object detection frameworks.

Q1: Novelty: The algorithm in the paper is strongly based on the network introduced by (Ren et al., 2015) with the domain adaptation strategy of (Chen et al., 2018; Saito et al., 2019)...

A1: Most of the previous domain adaptive object detection methods are based on some general object detection frameworks like YOLO, Faster RCNN, SSD, etc. So we think this should not be a drawback for us to adapt for the domain adaptive object detection task, unless we can develop a new one for general object detection but we think it’s not necessary to do that, also it’s not easy to propose a totally new one. For the differences to DA, strong-weak alignment and h-Detach, we have given a detailed explanation for R2, but we still want to clarify them here.

There are two main components proposed in this paper: 1) Stacked Complementary Losses and 2) Gradient Detach Updating.

Each component, if taken alone, SCL may be a little similar to strong-weak alignment and MAF if compared with them roughly, since they also use multi-objective for training. However, the inside design and motivation are totally different: Our method is motivated from deep supervision, but we make a further step to adapt multiple and diverse losses. content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I made a quick assessment of this paper.
content.review:
In this paper, a domain adaptive object detection model is proposed. It mainly includes two additional components : 1) stacked complementary loss, which includes multiple adversarial losses on intermediate layers, and a instance-context alignment loss at the final layer; 2) a gradient detach strategy to stop the backpropagation to  intermediate layers through the context features. Experiments are conducted on several benchmarks to valid their claims.

The paper is well written, and easy to follow. It shows good performance on a number of benchmark datasets. Overall, this is an incremental work. While the tricks discussed in the paper sounds reasonable, it provides very limited insights into the domain adaptive object detection problem,
1) complementary loss: actually, applying adversarial training on multiple levels have been discussed in the literature. For example, in the CAN model [Zhang et al., 2018], they append domain discriminators on different layers, and automatically learn if GRL layer should be activated or not. In DA-Faster-RCNN and SWDA, the authors used two levels of adversarial training. And in the recent MAF work [He and Zhang 2019], they also applied adversarial trainings on multiple levels. From those works, it can be seen that applying multiple adversarial trainings help to improve the adaptation, and carefully tuning the strengths of adversarial trainings would gain further improvements. For example, in CAN, they found the lower layers favors non-adversarial trainings or smaller weights for adversarial loss. Similarly, in SWDA, they observed that a weak alignment at higher layer with FL, and a strong alignment at lower layer with LS gives improvement. This paper also discussed different configurations for loss types on different layers, however, the designs basically followed the above existing works, and the observations are also similar.  
[Zhang et al. 2018] Zhang et al. Collaborative and Adversarial Network for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation. In CVPR  2018. 
[He and Zhang 2019] He and Zhang. Multi-adversarial Faster-RCNN for Unrestricted Object Detection. In ICCV 2019. 
2) context loss has also been discussed in SWDA, where they augmented the features from discriminators to instance features for a more stable training. In this paper, they used a different way to use the features from different conv-layers, however, this looks quite arbitrary. It is desirable to give more explanations on what motivates authors, and discussion and comparison to SWDA’s strategy are necessary.   
3) gradient detech has also been exploited. In SWDA, the gradient w.r.t. context features are also detached in the backpropagation for a stable training. However, neither SWDA nor this work present a convincing explanation on why gradient detach should help the adaptation. I noted that authors provided discussions in Section 4, but those observations are trivial. Could you explain how those gradients would demagage the model if no gradient detach is applied, and why? 

Further questions: 
1) Moreover, the experimental results are also inconsistent in some cases. For example, 
In table 1, ILoss(FL)+detach does not always give improvements. In the first group,  LS+LS+FL+X+X gives 35.0, while LS+LS+FL+FL+detach gives 34.9; in the second group, LS+FL+FL+X+X gives 35.5, while LS+FL+FL+FL+detach gives 35.5; in the last group,  LS+CE+FL+X+X gives 35.3, while LS+CE+FL+FL+detach gives 37.9. It seems the proposed ILoss+detach is quite tricky technique, it works only when they use LS+CE+FL, but performs in an opposite way for other settings. This means people should carefully design their models for using this trick. There are also a few cases of ablation studies missed in Table 1, for example, there is no corresponding “w/o detach version” of LS+FL+FL+FL+detach, making it difficult to valid if the detach generally helps.  I suggest the authors reorganize Table 1, and complete the missing cases, to verify their claims on complementary loss, context loss, and gradient detach separately and thoroughly. 

2) Similar ablation studies on other settings like PASCAL VOC->Clip Arts, Kitti->Cityscapes and INIT are needed. Cityscapes -> Foggy Cityscapes is a relatively speicial case, since the foggy images are synthesized images. 

3) There are a few works in CVPR 2019 and ICCV 2019, which provides state-of-the-art domain adaptation object detection performance. Those works should be included in experimental comparison, and carefully discussed.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2 [2/2]
content.comment:
Below we make further clarification and responses to each question of yours:
Q1: provides very limited insights...
A1: We have updated a new version with more insightful discussion, including: 1) why LS-CE-FL-FL + detach is the optimal combination; 2) the explanation of gradient detach; etc. We will continue revising our paper according to the reviewers’ feedback and suggestions.

Q2: complementary loss		 				
A2: We agree that complementary loss alone is not novel, but in this paper, we focus on stacking diverse objectives, not simply applying complementary loss in the framework.

Q3: context loss & gradient detach have also been exploited; explain how those gradients would damage the model if no gradient detach is applied, and why? 
A3: We agree that context loss, i.e. instance-context alignment loss has been explored with a similar shape in prior work (DA), but our contribution in this paper settles on the point of stacking diverse losses. For the gradient detach, it’s hard to say “w/o detach” will damage the model or not since some “w/o detach” models still work well, but it’s obvious that the learned features will not be discriminative enough as detach-based models. Also as shown in Fig. 6&8, if comparing with two heatmaps, it can be seen that “w/o detach” model focuses more on background (green color) as compared to with detach model (blue color, i.e., less attention).

Q4: results are inconsistent in some cases, reorganize Table 1, and complete the missing cases.
A4: Thanks very much for pointing out this. But we think this phenomenon cannot derive the conclusion that ILoss+detach is tricky. It indicates that “LS” (Least-squares Loss) can only be placed on the low-level features (rich spatial information and poor semantic information) and “FL” should be in the high-level locations (weak spatial information and strong semantic information). For the middle location, “CE” will be a good choice. If you use “LS” for the middle/high-level features or use “FL” on the low-level features, it will confuse the network to learn hierarchical semantic outputs, so that ILoss+detach will lose effectiveness under that circumstance. We think this is reasonable and also natural for domain adaptive object detection. We have reorganized Table 1 to make it more clear. Please check it out there.

For the missing case: LL_FL_FL_FL+w/o detach, we obtain the results:
bus: 0.416  bicycle: 0.309  car: 0.442  motorcycle: 0.292  person: 0.263  rider: 0.428  train: 0.364  truck: 0.267   mAP: 0.348  and have added it in the revision (more experiments are running and will be included soon).

Q5: Similar ablation studies on other settings.
A5: Thanks for this valuable suggestion which can definitely enhance the paper and make it more convincing. Actually, we have provided ablation studies of PASCAL VOC-->Clipart (Table 10) and PASCAL VOC-->WaterColor (Table 9) in our Appendix. We will add more but considering the length of the paper and we have already provided extensive ablation results in the main content, we will still put the new results into the Appendix after we finish them.

Q6: There are a few works in CVPR 2019 and ICCV 2019, which provides state-of-the-art domain adaptation object detection performance. Those works should be included in experimental comparison, and carefully discussed. 
A6: Thanks for this suggestion, we have tried our best to include and compare (in Table 1, 4, etc.) more of the related papers in the recent CVPR and ICCV in our revision, but we observe some papers use different degrees of FoggyCityscapes [1, 2] and experimental settings, which cannot be compared directly (even our result is better). Our experiments and results are from a unified code base and parameter settings, so we think our results will be more solid and reliable. We will continue revising this part to make it more comprehensive.

[1] Qi Cai, Yingwei Pan, Chong-Wah Ngo, Xinmei Tian, Lingyu Duan, and Ting Yao. "Exploring Object Relation in Mean Teacher for Cross-Domain Detection." In CVPR, 2019.
[2] Khodabandeh, M., Vahdat, A., Ranjbar, M. and Macready, W.G., 2019. A Robust Learning Approach to Domain Adaptive Object Detection. arXiv preprint arXiv:1904.02361.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2 [1/2]
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewer for your insightful and detailed comments, and constructive suggestions which definitely can help us to improve this paper. We think the biggest concern from you (also the other two reviewers) is the novelty/insight in this paper. So we would like to make further clarification about it. 

Essentially, there are two main components proposed in this paper: 1) Stacked Complementary Losses and 2) Gradient Detach Updating. 

Each component, if taken alone, 1) may be similar to strong-weak alignment and MAF to some extent if compared with them roughly, since they also use multi-objective for training. However, the inside design and motivation are totally different: Our method is motivated from deep supervision, but we make a further step to adapt multiple and diverse losses. In contrast, strong-weak adopted local and global branches and hasn’t explored whether stacked losses can further help to optimize the model. MAF applied multi-loss on Block 3, Block 4, Block 5 with the same formulation. As we mentioned in the abstract and introduction, this design cannot deliver a sufficient integration within different domains in the shallow layers. Thus, our work is truly deeper than all of these literature. 

From our results we can get the insight that domain adaptive object detection is supported by deep supervision, however, the diverse supervisions should be applied in a controlled manner.

2) is completely new and novel for this task. We didn’t find any previous work that has the same or relevant definition of it for domain adaptive object detection. The closest work may be the h-DETACH while it has a quite different manner and motivation with an irrelevant problem (sequential tasks) of our work. We observe this operation can help to learn more discriminative features after we have studied and visualized a very large variety of heatmaps, also we aim to maximize the information of context from the raw images to help the detector. Strong-weak chooses to use features after GRL layer, which may weaken the strength of information from the image. The proposed operation is simple, but it is very effective and efficient to achieve our goal. We tend to keep our method as simple as possible so that it can make a wide benefit/usage for other researches.
Also, gradient detach updating is the optimal companion for stacked complementary losses and they are complementary in our whole framework, our title also reflects this fact.

Furthermore, our result is competitive which outperforms the strong-weak alignment (CVPR’19) and MAF (ICCV’19) on the popular FoggyCityscapes benchmark by absolute 3.6%  and 3.9% mAP (Although R1 thinks ~3% mAP is not a large margin, we consider this as a fairly significant improvement.). This demonstrates that our design is a more reasonable choice than MAF and Strong-Weak method. We think how to use the correct way in designing a complicated framework to obtain desired performance should also be a novel point and important contribution to this task,  and it can even benefit the whole community (as we have released the code).
